                    ### Question
                    We have two tests to diagnose a serious prognosis disease. Test A has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 60% and test B has a sensitivity of 70% and a specificity of 99%. We have an effective treatment but that produces important adverse effects and also has a very high cost. What test would we choose to make the diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Test A because it will detect less false positives.
opb. Test A because it has a higher sensitivity.
opc. Test B because it will detect more false positives.
opd. Test A because it will detect more false negatives.
ope. Test B because it has a greater specificity.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In diagnosing a serious prognosis disease, the choice of test should prioritize sensitivity and specificity based on the clinical context. Test A has a sensitivity of 95%, which means it is effective at detecting true positives and minimizing false negatives, crucial for serious diseases where missing a diagnosis can have severe consequences. However, it has a specificity of 60%, leading to a higher rate of false positives. Test B, on the other hand, has a lower sensitivity of 70% but a much higher specificity of 99%, resulting in fewer false positives but a risk of missing some true cases. Given the serious nature of the disease and the importance of detecting all potential cases, Test A is preferred despite its lower specificity. The reasoning aligns with the consensus that in serious conditions, high sensitivity is prioritized to avoid false negatives. Therefore, the best choice is Test A due to its higher sensitivity, which is critical in this context.
